extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, and designers interested in aesthetic and practical principles of monumental and Gothic architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for designing and judging buildings with emphasis on masonry, the treatment of surfaces, and the management of light and shadow to achieve grandeur and unity. Covers massing, ornament restraint, material honesty, tracery, mouldings, and practical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate masonry sizing and accommodation
rubrics_metrics.description: Masonry should "accommodate itself, naturally and frankly, to the conditions and structure of its work" rather than be systematically very large or very small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using materials systematically small or large; masonry that adapts to situation shows power in both vast masses and fine work. Examples: mountain cottages use large stones integrated into walls; façades built of many small equal stones (e.g., St. Madeleine, Paris) can look like a close trellis and diminish dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the material when deciding on finishing (polish vs. rough)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a 'certain respect for material': softer stones (marble, limestones) invite delicate, polished work; hard stones (granite, lava) are often better left roughly squared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not needlessly smooth and polish stone where its natural cleavage and texture contribute to magnificence. Smoothing granite can show power but is generally costly and less wise than using that labor elsewhere. 'It will be well to take advantage of the stone's softness' for limestone; for granite 'it is wiser to make the design granitic itself, and to leave the blocks rudely squared.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of finish — avoid wasteful chiselling and polishing
rubrics_metrics.description: The sums wasted in chiselling and polishing stones which would be better left as quarried could instead accomplish larger works (e.g., raise a building an extra story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize substantive mass and height over unnecessary surface refinement. Anti-pattern: spending excessive labor on smoothing at the expense of scale and structural ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide surfaces into masses, not scattered lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The divisions of design should be 'either into masses of light and shade, or else by traced lines' — but mass-division (broad areas of light/dark) is generally paramount for value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No design that is divided at all and is not divided into masses can be of value. Masses should be large and bold enough to resist twilight and deep enough to avoid being flattened by noon sun. Linear division (pure linear division) is a specific mode (e.g., Henry VII's chapel panelling) and must be intentionally chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think in shadow — shadow is an architect's chief means of sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive shade is more necessary and more sublime in architecture than in painting; an architect must 'think in shadow' and conceive a design as it will be in dawn, dusk, heat and cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should plan how lights and shadows will fall, ensuring shadows provide human sympathy and express sorrow/mystery. Practice conceiving the building under varying light conditions and use shadow 'as men dig wells in unwatered plains.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Throw quantities of light and shade into coherent masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantities of shade or light must be thrown into masses either of roughly equal weight or by large masses relieved with small ones; masses are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid designs divided into many small or scattered patches of light/dark. Ensure masses are broad and clear so one does not get 'swallowed up by twilight' or 'dried like a shallow pool.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mass (form-bearing) from interval (background)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict 'mass' to portions to which proper form belongs, and call the field on which such forms are traced the 'interval' — this distinction is crucial to style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two marked styles depend on this: forms drawn with light upon darkness (Greek) and forms drawn with darkness upon light (early Gothic). Choice affects whether gradation or flat, trenchant shadow is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gradation for rounded (light) masses; seek breadth and diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 'light, or rounded, mass' tradition (Greek/Byzantine), aim for pure gradation and rounded surfaces so that light diffuses and forms are read by subtle modelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek workmen made figures readable by contrastring them against dark fields; Byzantine ornaments used gradation to achieve masculine breadth. Emphasize softened, full manner over sharp edged lines; natural analogues: clouds, mountains, tree crowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use flat, trenchant treatment for dark masses when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 'dark mass' or foil style (e.g., early Gothic tracery), designs are drawn as darkness upon light with flat darks and sharp terminations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This style characterizes a trenchant mode where darks and lights are flat and terminated by sharp edges. When employing it, ensure the darks are shaped and placed to carry the composition's power (e.g., Italian traceries where the dark penetrations form the whole effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep ornament subordinate to the purity of mass and tracery
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow surface ornament to disturb the simplicity and force of dark masses or the plan—ornament should often be 'merely added grace' and should not obscure the anatomy of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In traceries and cusps, avoid knots of flowerwork or intrusive sculpture that interfere with the black leaves or quatrefoils which should read from afar. Example: Giotto's work—mark the black spots rather than reify every carved detail. Anti-pattern: ornament so elaborate that the main effect is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat glass carefully in tracery — prefer open lights or recess glass
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass can 'spoil all traceries'; in the finest instances traceries are open lights, or the glass is set behind the tracery, casting clean shadows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When glazing is necessary, set glass well within the tracery to avoid diminishing shadow depth; where possible reserve delicate tracery for unglazed situations. Glazing sometimes used to slenderize lines but often reduces the intended shadow effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve breadth and rounded serenity in mouldings; avoid line-substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier mouldings were composed of alternate square and cylindrical shafts emphasizing broad surfaces and gradation; over time sharp fillets and lines supplanted mass and roundedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the corrupting progression where ridgy processes become definitive fillets and concavities deepen until the moulding becomes a series of concavities edged by delicate fillets on which the eye rests. Maintain gradation and the sculptural 'back' of forms rather than letting sharp lines dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the corrupting principle: multiplication of small details that destroy mass
rubrics_metrics.description: When penetrative ornaments multiply, becoming shallower and running together, they lose individual character and the Gothic power falls by replacement of mass with line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist tendencies to multiply tiny penetrations, twigs, or punched holes that 'run together' like bubbles—this results in scattered detail and a loss of broad effect. The historical pattern: bold penetrations → shallower/multiplication → running together → loss of mass and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curved surfaces demand serenity and careful rounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Curved surfaces require even more serenity and breadth; some curvature is necessary to secure grandeur in small masses of light, and perception of rounded surface is a high mark of skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many noble forms use subdued curvature; artists differ in their delicacy of perception of rounded surface. Practice expressing perspective, foreshortening and undulation in subordinate masses to preserve serenity and truth to Nature. Example: rendering of tree foliage depends on securing ruling rounded form first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of mass and breadth as the decisive attribute of majesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative majesty of buildings depends more on the weight and vigor of their masses than on any other attribute: 'mass of everything, of bulk, of light, of darkness, of color... breadth of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the chief practical rule: prefer solid stone, broad sunshine, starless shade; avoid broken light, scattered darkness, or divided weight. Apply this to every feature, however trifling, because mass/breadth can give power everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical avoidance of small repetitive elements that conflict with main lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce small repetitive carpentry or cross-bars which multiply lines and contradict the architecture's primary directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: wooden fillings of belfry lights divided into many cross-bars multiply horizontal lines and are uninteresting; prefer three or four penthouse roofs creating four or five grand masses of shadow, which harmonize with architecture and may be more delightful than stone-work itself.
